# Game

[Framework](README.md) · `DotGame.Framework` · class

```csharp
public abstract class Game : IDisposable
```

The base class of a game: its services, the display it draws to, and the hooks it overrides to load, update, draw, and respond to the app's lifecycle.

## Remarks

A platform runs the game through a `GameHost`, which owns the sequencing: when each hook runs, what a pause or stop during startup does, and how frames are timed. This class holds only what a game sees, and the internal members the host calls.

## Constructors

```csharp
protected Game()
```

Makes the game. Its services don't exist until [`OnInitialize`](#oninitialize).

### DisplayDpi

```csharp
public float DisplayDpi { get; }
```

Effective display density in physical dots-per-inch, as reported by the host platform. Used by gesture recognizers and other UI code that needs thresholds expressed in physical units (e.g. millimeters). Defaults to 96 DPI (the historical desktop baseline) until the platform reports a real value.

### FirstFrameDrawn

```csharp
public Task FirstFrameDrawn { get; }
```

Completes once the first frame since starting has been drawn. Start work the first frame doesn't need after it, such as signing in, syncing, or analytics: on the web the game shares the page's only thread, so work started earlier delays the first frame even when nothing awaits it. Continuations run on the game thread in a later frame.

### FixedUpdateRate

```csharp
public int? FixedUpdateRate { get; set; }
```

How many times a second of game time [`OnFixedUpdate`](#onfixedupdate) runs, or null for it not to run at all, which is the default, so that a game that doesn't use it pays nothing for it. Unlike [`PreferredFrameRate`](#preferredframerate), it's not a preference, and it has nothing to do with the display. A game usually sets it once, in its constructor.

**Throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`:** The value isn't positive.

### PreferredFrameRate

```csharp
public int? PreferredFrameRate { get; set; }
```

The frame rate the game would like, or null for the display's own, which is the default. A casual game can ask for 30 or 60 on a fast display, for the battery, and it can change at any time, such as to run menus slower than play. It's a preference: the desktop and the web draw at most this many frames a second, unevenly if it doesn't divide into the display's rate, and Android and iOS ask the system, which has the last word. It says what the game asked for, not the rate it's getting.

**Throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`:** The value isn't positive.

### PreferredMultisampleCount

```csharp
public int PreferredMultisampleCount { get; set; }
```

The samples per pixel the game would like, to smooth the edges of rotated quads, from 1 for none, which is the default. It's a preference: a device may give fewer, and `Graphics.MultisampleCount` says what it gave. Set it in the game's constructor, as the graphics device is made with it. Render textures aren't multisampled, so a game drawing its scene through one gets no benefit.

**Throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`:** The value is below 1.

**Throws `InvalidOperationException`:** The game's services already exist.

### RunWhenInactive

```csharp
public bool RunWhenInactive { get; set; }
```

Whether the game keeps running while it's inactive. An inactive game (its window lost focus, or something covers it) stops game time and [`OnUpdate`](#onupdate), and keeps its picture correct; set this for a game that should keep going instead, such as one played on a second monitor. A hidden game stops drawing either way.

Runs once a frame: draw everything. Draw only, as a hidden game skips it.

### OnFixedUpdate

```csharp
protected virtual void OnFixedUpdate()
```

Runs [`FixedUpdateRate`](#fixedupdaterate) times a second of game time, for physics and anything that must behave the same at any frame rate: none, one or several times a frame, before [`OnUpdate`](#onupdate). It doesn't run until that rate is set, which build rule DG0005 checks. `Time.DeltaSeconds` is the step's length here, and [`TimeService.FixedAlpha`](TimeService.md#fixedalpha) smooths drawing between steps.

### OnGamepadEvent

```csharp
protected virtual void OnGamepadEvent(GamepadEvent gamepadEvent)
```

Types: [`GamepadEvent`](GamepadEvent.md)

A gamepad connecting, disconnecting or changing, before [`OnUpdate`](#onupdate). Events that arrive while the game is starting are dropped, so read `Input.GetGamepadState` for what's already connected.

### OnLowMemory

```csharp
protected virtual void OnLowMemory()
```

The system is short of memory and may end the app: release what can be loaded again. Not every platform reports this. Runs on the game thread.

### OnPause

```csharp
protected virtual Task OnPause()
```

The game has become inactive: its window lost focus, something covers it, or the app went to the background. An app can be ended without warning from here, so save now. Work this awaits runs on, including while the game is hidden, within what the platform allows (a few seconds on iOS and on a hidden web page); game time doesn't, so don't wait on `Time.DelayAsync` here.
